To determine if memory-provoked regional cerebral blood flow (rCBF)-spectrum positron emission tomography (rCBF-SPECT) is a useful diagnostic tool in Alzheimer's disease, we need to consider its performance in detecting AD-related changes in the brain at both the group and individual levels.

Studies have shown that memory provocation can increase the sensitivity of rCBF-SPECT for detecting alterations in blood flow associated with Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, further research is needed to evaluate the diagnostic potential of MP-SPECT (multicenter positron emission tomography) as a standalone tool in AD diagnosis. Currently, MP-SPECT may be sufficient in clinical settings if sensitivity for diagnosing AD at an individual level can be verified in future studies.

In summary, while memory provocation increased the sensitivity of rCBF-SPECT for detecting AD-related blood flow changes, more research is required to establish its utility as a diagnostic tool for Alzheimer's disease diagnosis.
